title: The Verdict Crowd
subtitle: An acquittal in a hit-and-run case brings the victim’s neighbourhood to the court steps
coldOpen: 14:00. The court acquits a driver in a hit-and-run case.
14:40. Three hundred from the victim’s lane reach the steps.
The judge is still in the building.

briefing.grievance: A boy from the transit lanes died under a car eighteen months ago. Today the driver walked free because two witnesses turned hostile. His neighbours believe the witnesses were bought and the court did not care.
knownFacts: The acquittal cites two witnesses who retracted their statements in court.
The prosecution has thirty days to appeal.
The judge and court staff are inside; the crowd fills the steps and the road.
unverifiedClaims: A post says the driver’s family paid the witnesses.
A message says the judge was transferred last week as a favour.
briefing.responsibility: You run the district administration. The court’s security and the crowd’s safety are both yours.
briefing.objective: Protect the court and the crowd, respect the verdict while pursuing the appeal, and give a grieving lane a lawful route.

rightsMoments.question: A court acquits a man the neighbourhood believes guilty. What does the rule of law require of the administration?

options.text: Protect the court and the acquitted man, pursue the lawful remedy (appeal, inquiry into the retractions), and protect witnesses so the next trial is fair.
options.feedback: Correct. Disagreement with a verdict is answered by appeal and investigation, never by force against the court or the acquitted.

options.text: Let the crowd express its justice; the court failed them.
options.feedback: A lynching is not justice; it destroys the only system that can correct a wrong verdict.

options.text: Order an inquiry into the judge to satisfy the crowd.
options.feedback: The executive cannot investigate a judge for a verdict; judicial independence is part of the rule of law.

rightsMoments.principle: The rule of law and judicial independence mean verdicts are challenged by appeal, witnesses are protected so trials can be fair, and the acquitted are protected like anyone else.
rightsMoments.why: The court’s own referral, an appeal with a date, and a sealed CCTV copy gave the lane a route; a rope would have ended every route.

simple.question: A court frees a man the lane believes is guilty. What must the state do?

options.a: Protect the court and the man. Appeal. Investigate the retractions. Protect witnesses.
options.b: Let the crowd have its justice.
options.c: Investigate the judge to calm the crowd.

feedback.a: Yes! Disagree with a verdict through appeal, never through force.
feedback.b: No. A lynching destroys the only system that can fix a wrong verdict.
feedback.c: The state cannot investigate a judge for a verdict.

simple.principle: Verdicts are challenged in court, not in the street. Witnesses and the acquitted are both protected.
simple.why: The court’s referral, an appeal with a date and a saved camera copy gave the lane a route. A rope ends every route.

improvements.text: Read the judgment before the crowd does; the court often agrees with them more than they think.
improvements.simple: Read the judgment to the crowd first.

improvements.text: Seventy-two hours is a deadline; treat it as one.
improvements.simple: Save the camera before it deletes.

improvements.text: Protect the acquitted as hard as you protect the court.

closing.good: The judge went home by the back door, the lane heard the referral from the front steps, the CCTV is sealed, and the appeal has a date.
closing.mixed: The court was protected and the appeal announced, but the witnesses are still unprotected and the footage is gone.
closing.poor: A grieving lane was beaten or an acquitted man was left to a rope, and the lawful route was never named.
